$comment: Which One Doesn't Belong sets, keyed by MCCRS standard. The defining property of a WODB set is that EVERY item can be argued as the odd one out — a set where only one answer is defensible is a multiple-choice question wearing a costume. `reasons[i]` is therefore not an answer key; it is the argument a student might not have found yet, revealed only after they commit to their own. tools/wodb.test.mjs enforces four items, four distinct non-empty reasons, and a standard that exists in data/ccss-standards.json.

reasons: It is the only one already written in simplest form.
It is the only one where both numbers are even.
It is the only one where both numbers are greater than 5.
It is the only one that is NOT equivalent to 2 : 3.
6.AT.1.teacherNote: Three of these are the same ratio in different clothes. Push for the word 'equivalent' before you confirm anything.

reasons: It is the only one where both numbers are multiples of 3.
It is the only one that costs less than $10.
It is the only one where the cost is a multiple of 10.
It is the only one whose unit rate is NOT $4 per pound.
6.AT.2.teacherNote: The unit rate is the argument you want, but let the surface-feature answers come first — they are what make the rate argument feel powerful.

reasons: It is the only one using the smallest amounts.
It is the only one where both numbers are odd.
It is the only one where the first number is a multiple of 4.
It is the only one that is NOT a 3 : 1 mix.
6.AT.3.teacherNote: Ask which two mixes would taste the same. That question does the ratio reasoning without the word 'ratio'.

6.AT.3a.prompt: Which pair doesn't belong in the table?
reasons: It is the only one with the smallest values.
It is the only one where both numbers are odd.
It is the only one where both numbers are multiples of 4.
It is the only one where the second number is NOT 5 times the first.
6.AT.3a.teacherNote: If a student says '(5, 24) is wrong', ask them what the rule is. Naming the rule is the whole lesson.

reasons: It is the only one with a two-digit conversion number smaller than 100.
It is the only one whose units both appear on another card.
It is the only metric conversion.
It is the only one that measures capacity instead of length.
6.AT.3c.teacherNote: The metric/customary split and the length/capacity split are different cuts through the same four cards. Both are correct.

reasons: It is the only one that means exactly half.
It is the only one whose percent is not a multiple of 10.
It is the only one where the whole is 200.
It is the only one whose value is NOT 20.
6.AT.4.teacherNote: Three of these equal 20. Let students discover that before you say it — the surprise is the point.

reasons: It is the only one whose value is less than 9.
It is the only one with an odd value.
It is the only one with a base of 4.
It is the only one with an exponent greater than 3.
6.AT.5.teacherNote: 4² and 2⁴ are both 16. That coincidence is worth two minutes on its own.

reasons: It is the only one that starts with the variable and adds.
It is the only one that starts with a number.
It is the only one with no addition or subtraction.
It is the only one where switching the order changes the value.
6.AT.6a.teacherNote: n + 5 and 5 + n are equal; n − 5 and 5 − n are not. That asymmetry is the idea hiding in this set.

6.AT.6c.prompt: If n = 4, which one doesn't belong?
reasons: It is the only one with a coefficient in front of the variable.
It is the only one where 4 is added.
It is the only one whose value is NOT 8 when n = 4.
It is the only one that gets smaller as n gets bigger.
6.AT.6c.teacherNote: Try n = 2 afterwards. Three of these stop agreeing, which is exactly why evaluating at one value proves nothing.

reasons: It is the only one written with parentheses.
It is the only one where the coefficient and the constant are both multiples of 3.
It is the only one written as a repeated sum.
It is the only one that is NOT equivalent to the other three.
6.AT.7.teacherNote: Substituting x = 1 settles the equivalence argument fast, and shows why 'it looks different' is not evidence.

reasons: It is the only one where both numbers shown are prime.
It is the only one with a coefficient.
It is the only subtraction equation.
It is the only one whose solution is NOT 4.
6.AT.8.teacherNote: Solve all four before arguing. Students who argue from the look of the equation instead of the solution are the ones to call on.

reasons: It is the only one whose smallest whole-number solution is 4.
It is the only one where 3 itself is a solution.
It is the only one that points the other way.
It is the only one that is not about 3.
6.AT.9.teacherNote: Ask whether x = 3 works for each one. The open/closed circle stops being a rule to memorize once they answer that.

items: How tall are the students in my class?
How many minutes did I sleep last night?
How many minutes do sixth graders sleep?
reasons: It is the only height question with just one answer.
It is the only statistical question about height.
It is the only time question with just one answer.
It is the only statistical question about time.
6.DS.1.teacherNote: This set is a 2×2: statistical or not, height or time. Both cuts are right, which is the cleanest way to show that 'statistical' is about variability, not topic.

reasons: It is the only one where every value is within 1 of the middle.
It is the only one where every value is odd.
It is the only one with no spread at all.
It is the only one with no repeated value.
6.DS.3.teacherNote: All four have a mean of 3. Compute that first, then ask what else you would want to know about a data set — that question is variability.

reasons: It is the only one that uses every value in a calculation.
It is the only one you find by putting the data in order.
It is the only one that must be a value from the data set.
It is the only one that is NOT a measure of center.
6.DS.4.teacherNote: Every one of these has a real argument. Do not let the room settle on 'range' as the right answer — take all four.

reasons: It is the only one where you can count every single data point.
It is the only one that groups numbers into intervals.
It is the only one built from the five-number summary.
It is the only one that shows categories instead of numbers.
6.DS.5.teacherNote: The histogram/bar-graph distinction is the one students most often miss, and it lands better as an argument than as a definition.

reasons: It is the only one affected by every value, including outliers.
It is the only center that resists outliers.
It is the only one that uses just the highest and lowest values.
It is the only one that describes only the middle half.
6.DS.6c.teacherNote: Two of these are centers and two are spreads, but each one also has its own argument. Sort them twice.

reasons: It is the only one that changes when any single value changes.
It is the only one that splits the data into two equal halves.
It is the only measure of variability.
It is the only one that can have more than one value for the same data set.
6.DS.6d.teacherNote: Ask which one you would report to someone who could only hear one number, and why. There is no single right answer, which is the point.

reasons: It is the only one where you have to divide by 2.
It is the only one whose two given lengths are consecutive numbers.
It is the only one with no right angles.
It is the only one whose area is NOT 12 square units.
6.GR.1.teacherNote: Three areas are 12. Ask how a triangle and a rectangle can cover the same space — that is the ×½ made physical.

reasons: It is the only one whose three edges are consecutive whole numbers.
It is the only one that is a single layer thick.
It is the only one with a square face.
It is the only one whose volume is NOT 24 cubic units.
6.GR.2.teacherNote: Same volume, different shapes. Build two of them with cubes if you can — the equality is much harder to believe than to verify.

reasons: It is the only one whose faces are all congruent.
It is the only one whose faces are all rectangles but not all the same.
It is the only one with exactly two triangular faces.
It is the only one that is not a prism.
6.GR.4.teacherNote: Sketch a net for each before arguing. The pyramid's net is the one that settles 'why is this different'.

reasons: It is the only one where both denominators are even.
It is the only one whose answer is NOT 2.
It is the only one that starts with a whole number.
It is the only one whose first numerator is 2.
6.NOS.1.teacherNote: Read each one aloud as 'how many of these fit into that?' Three of them fit exactly twice, which makes the fourth stand out for a reason students can feel.

reasons: It is the only one where the divisor and the quotient are the same.
It is the only one whose dividend is less than 140.
It is the only one whose dividend is greater than 150.
It is the only one that does NOT divide evenly.
6.NOS.2.teacherNote: Estimate before dividing. A student who spots that 144 is not a multiple of 11 without computing is doing exactly the right thing.

reasons: It is the only one that uses addition.
It is the only one already written as a single number.
It is the only one written as a fraction.
It is the only one that uses multiplication.
6.NOS.3.teacherNote: All four equal 0.75. Every argument here is about REPRESENTATION, not value — which is the whole reason this set is worth doing.

reasons: It is the only one that is a factor of two of the others.
It is the only one that is not a multiple of 4.
It is the only one that is a multiple of 8.
It is the only perfect square.
6.NOS.4.teacherNote: List the factors of all four on the board first. The arguments come out of the lists on their own.

reasons: It is the only negative integer.
It is the only positive number.
It is the only one that is not an integer.
It is the only one that is neither positive nor negative.
6.NOS.6.teacherNote: Place all four on one number line before arguing. 0 being its own opposite is the idea most worth chasing here.

reasons: It is the only one with both coordinates positive.
It is the only one with a negative x and a positive y.
It is the only one with a positive x and a negative y.
It is the only one with both coordinates negative.
6.NOS.7.teacherNote: Plot all four. Each is a reflection of another across an axis — ask which mirror turns one into another.

reasons: It is the only one where the bars actually change the value.
It is the only one written with no symbols at all.
It is the only one that does NOT equal 5.
It is the only one where the bars are there but change nothing.
6.NOS.8.teacherNote: Three of these are 5. Ask what absolute value bars DO, not what they mean — the answer is 'distance from zero', and this set makes that necessary.

reasons: It is the only one on the y-axis and not at the origin.
It is the only one on the x-axis and not at the origin.
It is the only one at the origin.
It is the only one that is not on an axis.
6.NOS.9.teacherNote: The order of the coordinates is what separates (0, 5) from (5, 0). If nobody raises it, plot them both and wait.
